History · 27 November 2026

The Stroop effect: when reading outruns looking

A simple task, naming the colour of the ink, published in 1935, has become one of the most robust findings in psychology.

Try saying out loud the colour of the ink of this word: RED. Almost everyone hesitates for a moment. The word says one thing and the colour another, and reading gets there first whether we like it or not. That small interference has been studied for almost a century and has a name of its own: the Stroop effect.

A doctoral experiment

John Ridley Stroop published it in 1935, based on his doctoral thesis at George Peabody College in Nashville. The idea had a history: in 1886 James McKeen Cattell, who had worked with Wundt in Leipzig, had already noticed that we read words faster than we name colours or objects. Stroop took the next step and set the two tasks against each other.

He prepared cards with colour names printed in a different ink ("blue" written in green, for example) and timed how long participants took to name the ink colour. Compared with naming the colour of plain squares, it took considerably longer. Reading the word while ignoring the ink, on the other hand, was barely affected. The automatic process, reading, interfered with the deliberate one, naming the colour; the reverse hardly happened at all.

Why it matters

The finding fitted an idea that cognitive psychology would develop decades later: with practice, some processes become automatic and run by themselves, while others need attentional control. A fluent adult reader cannot "switch off" reading. Children who are still learning to read show less interference, precisely because reading is not yet automatic for them.

In 1991 Colin MacLeod reviewed half a century of research and counted hundreds of studies. The effect appears very reliably, across languages and in many variants: emotional words, numbers, pictures with words printed over them. When psychology spent the last decade checking which of its classic results held up, the Stroop effect came out very well.

From the laboratory to the clinic

Versions of the task are now part of many neuropsychological batteries, because they help assess attention and inhibitory control, functions that depend largely on the frontal lobes. As with any test, a single score diagnoses nothing: it is interpreted alongside the person's history and other assessments, always by professionals.

An everyday lesson

The Stroop effect is a useful reminder outside the lab too: whatever we have practised a lot takes over by default. That is why well-worn habits are so hard to change, and why it helps to shape our surroundings, remove distractions and not rely on willpower alone.

References

  1. Stroop, J. R. (1935). Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 18(6), 643–662.
  2. Cattell, J. M. (1886). The time it takes to see and name objects. Mind, 11(41), 63–65.
  3. MacLeod, C. M. (1991). Half a century of research on the Stroop effect: An integrative review. Psychological Bulletin, 109(2), 163–203.
